critique.good: The metric column is generous (139px), so every row label wraps cleanly at word boundaries in 1–3 lines and the first column reads as a proper row index. Row rhythm is compact (650px tall) and the table stays inside the 360px box.
critique.problems: The four period columns are destroyed: headers break into 'FY / 202 / 2' with digits torn apart, and values break into '$1,8 / 40', '$31 / 8.4 / M', '$41. / 2M'. 26 mid-word splits make numbers unreadable and the four period columns no longer compare as a band — column heights become wildly uneven (83/106/129) because split numbers push rows taller.
critique.cause: 55px per period column leaves only 34px of text width. '2022' needs ~38px and the widest numeric token ($318.4M, $101.3M) needs ~63px, so both headers and values are forced to split. The 139px given to col 1 was taken out of the columns that hold the data.

critique.good: Header row is now stable ('FY 2022' etc. on one line) and col 1 at 103px is the true minimum that keeps metric words like 'acquisition' and 'percentage' whole. Table still fits exactly in 360px.
critique.problems: Numbers are still shredded: '$1,84 / 0', '$318. / 4M', '$41.2 / M', '$101. / 3M' — 17 splits. Rows balloon to 153px and the table grows to 813px tall, so the numeric band reads as ragged text rather than a column of comparable figures; the eye cannot compare $1,840 against $1,655 because the digits are stacked differently in each cell.
critique.cause: 64px per period column = 43px of text. That is under the ~47px needed for '$1,840' and far under the ~63px needed for '$318.4M'/'$101.3M'. Only the header token happens to fit; every longer number must break.

critique.good: The best numeric band of the three: headers on one line, values like $1,840 / $1,765 / $1,690 / $1,655 aligned as single tokens, row heights consistent, only 2 residual splits. Comparison across FY 2022–FY 2024 works exactly as intended.
critique.problems: The table is 432px wide and overflows the pink box by 72px, so the entire Q1 2025 column (the newest period, the one a reader most wants) is cut off mid-number ('12', '74', '$5…'). The table also loses its outer right border visually. A table whose latest period is hidden defeats its purpose.
critique.cause: 103px (minimum for whole metric words) + 4×82px (minimum for one-line headers) = 432px, which simply exceeds 359px. The overflow is structural, not a tuning error.

critique.good: The four period columns are equal, which correctly signals that FY 2022–Q1 2025 are one peer group; the metric column is clearly separated as a row index. Row banding and borders read cleanly, so rows are easy to follow.
critique.problems: The table is 813px tall and each metric row is 3–6 lines, so the eye can no longer scan down the metric column or across a row. Values are broken mid-token ($318.4 / M, $548.1 / M, 121 / %), headers stack into 4–5 fragments (FY / 202 / 2), and the whole table is clipped 48px past the box.
critique.cause: The metric column is fixed at 103px (82px of text) — barely one unbreakable word — while the period columns get only 76px (55px of text), less than the 61–63px their values need. Both columns are too narrow for their content, so every cell wraps, inflating height and splitting numbers.

critique.good: Equal 80px period columns keep the value band rhythmic, and a few more values now fit ($1,840, 71.3%, 38.2%), so some rows read at a glance.
critique.problems: Still 813px tall with 6-line metric rows; the widest values ($318.4M, $402.7M, $511.9M, $101.2M) still split and the Q1 2025 column is cut off at the right edge. The extra 4px per period column bought almost nothing visually.
critique.cause: 80px gives 59px of text, still under the ~63px the money values need; meanwhile the metric column remains at 103px, so the dominant cause of the height — the 407px of label squeezed into 82px — was left untouched.

critique.good: 84px period columns are the first design that works for the numbers: every value stays on one line, headers read as single lines (FY 2022, Q1 2025), and there are no mid-word splits. The table drops to 790px and looks calm and regular.
critique.problems: The metric column still produces 6-line rows, so the table is nearly as tall as r1A; and because nothing was given to the labels, the width went entirely into the periods, pushing the table 80px out of the box — the Q1 2025 column is mostly clipped. Reading a row means horizontal scrolling before you can even see the value.
critique.cause: Spending all available width on the four period columns (4×84=336) while keeping the metric column at 103px fixes the values but leaves the real bottleneck (a 407px label column) unsolved, and 103+336=440 cannot fit in 360.

critique.good: The four period columns are equal at 84px, so headers stay on one line and all numeric tokens remain intact; the metric column at 176px keeps most row labels to 2–4 lines, making rows relatively easy to scan vertically.
critique.problems: The table is 513px wide and overflows the 360px box by 153px, hiding FY 2024 and Q1 2025 almost entirely. That defeats the table’s core purpose: comparing six metrics across four periods. The metric column also dominates the layout, and the 106px-tall sales-and-marketing row creates a conspicuous break in the row rhythm.
critique.cause: 176 + 4×84 = 512px. The period band is already at its practical minimum, so the entire excess comes from giving the metric column 176px when only about 103px is needed to keep its longest word intact.

critique.good: The wider 224px metric column gives the cleanest row-label reading: most labels fit in 2–3 lines, the table is shorter at 394px, and the period headers and values are completely unbroken.
critique.problems: At 561px it overflows by 201px, so only FY 2022 and FY 2023 are fully visible; the later periods, which are the newest and often most important, require scrolling. The metric column is now 40% of the table width, giving labels more visual weight than the data itself.
critique.cause: 224 + 4×84 = 560px. The metric column was expanded well beyond what the labels require, while the period columns are correctly held at their no-wrap minimum.

critique.good: This is the most balanced of the three: the 150px metric column keeps labels to 3–5 lines, the 86px period columns are comfortable, all headers stay on one line, and there are no mid-word splits. The table feels less label-dominated than r2B.
critique.problems: It still overflows by 135px, so FY 2024 is only partly visible and Q1 2025 is off-screen. The 129px-tall sales-and-marketing row and 5-line labels create uneven row heights and slow down horizontal comparison.
critique.cause: 150 + 4×86 = 494px. Both the metric column and the period columns carry avoidable slack: the metric column could lose about 22px before its longest word would split, and each period column has 2–5px more than its one-line content needs.

understanding.purpose: A compact operating and financial KPI table for comparing six metrics across FY 2022, FY 2023, FY 2024 and Q1 2025; readers use it to scan trends over time rather than read prose.
understanding.reading: Scan the first column down to find the metric, then read across the four period columns to compare values. The metric column is the row index; the four period columns form a matched numeric band. Long metric labels will wrap at word boundaries, and period headers can stack as FY / 2022 and Q1 / 2025, but digits and currency/percent tokens should not split.
groups: Column 1: row-label/index column, separate from all values.

Columns 2–5: one peer group of period-value columns; equal width is appropriate because they play the same role and support across-row comparison. Q1 2025 is a shorter latest period but still belongs to this band.
keep_intact: Metric names' unbreakable words such as 'percentage', 'acquisition' and 'recurring' — no mid-word splits
Numeric values including $, commas, decimals and % (e.g. $1,800, 71.3%)
Year digits 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025 — headers may break only after 'FY' or 'Q1'
may_wrap: Long metric labels at spaces or commas, over 2–4 lines
Period headers into two lines: FY / 2022, Q1 / 2025
Header rows and metric rows may grow taller; numeric body cells should stay on one line

bad.why: The 80px data columns force 4/5 headers to wrap and cause three mid-word splits, breaking values such as $318.4M into separate lines and destroying numeric comparability.
The 103px metric column collapses long row labels into 5–6-line word stacks, making the table 790px tall while the numeric columns sit mostly empty; rows stop reading as phrases.
Essentially the same fault as r1C: a 104px metric column produces one-word-per-line row headers and excessive vertical sprawl for a table whose data cells are short.
The 224px metric column over-prioritizes labels; at 360px only one full year column is visible, so comparing years requires repeated horizontal scrolling and the row header scrolls away.

final.rationale: This is a row-header comparison table: the metric column carries phrases, while the four year columns are interchangeable numeric roles. r2A gives the metric column enough width to keep labels to 2–4 lines and gives each year column just enough width to keep headers and values such as $318.4M intact, producing a compact 487px-tall table with a clear roughly 2:1 hierarchy. It overflows by 153px, but the alternatives either force one-word-per-line row labels or push so much of the year series off-screen that comparison becomes cumbersome. r1B is clearly unacceptable because its narrow data columns split numeric identifiers and wrap headers.

general: Size a row-header column by the longest natural phrase it must carry; equal widths across all columns usually misallocate space.
For numeric or date columns, set width from the longest unbreakable token plus padding; below that, values and headers split and the table loses integrity.
On narrow screens, horizontal overflow can be the lesser evil, but only if the row header plus enough comparable data columns remain visible; otherwise comparison breaks.
Avoid tall, sparse rows created by one-word-per-line wrapping; a wider label column often buys more scanning speed than it costs in overflow.
specific: The minimum no-split width here is about 440px (103 + 4×84), so every valid design must overflow 360px; the real choice is how much extra width to trade for shorter rows.
The four year columns need about 84px each; 80px splits values and headers, while 86–90px adds little.
The metric column needs roughly 168–190px to avoid the 5–6-line word stacks seen at 103–120px.
r2A's 176px metric column is the best balance; r2B's 224px is too wide for the comparative task.

final.tradeoffs: Horizontal scrolling versus vertical height: r1C/r3A keep three year columns visible initially but make rows very tall, while r2A accepts fewer visible years for readable labels and compact rows. Some designers may prefer r3B's smaller 105px overflow over r2A's 153px.
final.uncertain: Exact range boundaries depend on browser line-breaking; whether r2B is publishable inside a horizontally scrollable container; whether r1C/r3A should be treated as bad or merely as an acceptable no-split fallback; whether the first column would remain sticky during horizontal scroll.

A.why: All columns fit, but the metric names break repeatedly inside words, making the row headers hard to read. Some monetary values and headers also wrap.

B.why: Metric names stay intact, but the narrow first column creates tall rows, several values and year headers wrap, and Q1 requires scrolling.

C.why: Metric names wrap naturally and values stay intact. The wider first column improves readability, though part of FY 2024 and all of Q1 require scrolling.

D.why: The first three years are mostly visible and monetary values stay on one line. The narrow metric column makes several rows tall, and FY 2024 wraps in its header.

E.why: Metric names wrap naturally with a comfortable rhythm, and the first three annual columns are largely visible with values intact. Q1 requires horizontal scrolling.

F.why: The generous metric column makes labels easy to scan and keeps rows compact, but only two full year columns fit initially, so comparing later periods requires more scrolling.

reviews.unsure: The screenshots show only the portion near the viewport edge, so the full width and appearance of the offscreen columns are difficult to judge.

A.why: The wide metric column keeps labels readable and rows reasonably compact. The numeric columns are clear, but the viewport shows only two complete periods and part of a third, so comparison requires scrolling.

B.why: Labels and values remain intact, and more of FY 2024 is visible than in A. The narrower metric column adds wrapping, especially to the longer labels, and the later periods still require scrolling.

C.why: The narrow metric column makes labels tall and difficult to scan, while the fiscal-year headings wrap and some monetary values split from their M suffix. The fourth period still requires scrolling.

D.why: All periods fit in the viewport, but the metric labels break inside words throughout, making row identification very difficult. Some monetary values also split from their M suffix.

E.why: Values stay intact, but the narrow metric column produces tall, heavily wrapped rows. The FY 2024 heading wraps while earlier headings do not, and the final period requires scrolling.

F.why: Metric labels wrap at word boundaries and remain fairly readable, while values stay intact. Nearly three annual columns are visible initially, giving useful comparison before scrolling to the final period.

reviews.unsure: The screenshots cut off the right side of several layouts, so the complete appearance of the final columns cannot be assessed. F appears to offer the strongest balance between readable row labels and initial visibility of annual comparisons.

A.why: Metric column squeezed to ~75px, so row labels break mid-word ("revenu e retenti on", "blende d", "month s") and numbers split too ("$318.4 M"); the table fits the box but is unreadable and comparison across years is destroyed.

B.why: Row labels wrap at word boundaries (4 lines) but numeric columns are too tight: headers break ("FY"/"2022") and amounts split from their unit ("$318.4"/"M"), and the Q1 2025 column is sliced in half at the edge with its header cut ("Q1 20…").

C.why: Clean word-level wrapping in the metric column, one-line headers, and values like "$318.4M" stay intact; cost is that FY 2024 is cut mid-column at the edge, so the reader scrolls without a clean stopping point.

D.why: Similar to B — 4-5 line row labels, one-line values for most rows, but "FY 2024" header wraps to two lines inconsistently and the Q1 column is cut through its header and values, reading as accidental clipping.

E.why: Best balance: metric column wide enough for tidy 3-4 line wraps at word boundaries, all three visible year headers on one line, every number intact ("$318.4M", "$92.5M"), and the edge falls exactly on the FY 2024 column boundary so the hidden Q1 column is a clean continuation rather than a sliced column.

F.why: Widest metric column gives the most readable row labels (2-3 lines) and keeps numbers whole, but it buys that by pushing FY 2024 and Q1 off-screen, so only two of four data columns are fully usable per screen.

reviewsOld.unsure: Whether a partially peeking column (C) should count as a helpful scroll affordance rather than a flaw, and whether F's wider label column is preferable if most reading is vertical (row-by-row) rather than across years.

A.why: Metric column is wide enough that labels wrap cleanly in 2–4 lines without splitting words; the year columns (~93px) keep every figure intact on one line ($318.4M, $1,690) and headers single-line. Row rhythm is even and the eye can run across the numbers; only the last column falls outside the box, which is unavoidable here and handled by scrolling.

B.why: Figures all stay intact and headers are on one line, but the Metric column is tighter (~120px) so the long labels stack 4–5 lines, making rows taller and less even than A; the third visible column is clipped mid-header ('FY 20'), which reads as an accident rather than a deliberate scroll point.

C.why: Squeezing the Metric column to ~80px forces 5–7 line labels while the year columns (~70px) break number+unit across lines ('$318.4' / 'M'), destroying the integrity of the identifiers; tall ragged rows make cross-row comparison of the figures hard.

D.why: The Metric column is so narrow (~55px) that words split mid-word ('revenu e', 'retenti on', 'month s', 'Custo mer', 'blende d'), and numbers are broken onto two lines everywhere; the table is effectively unreadable and the row unit collapses.

E.why: Values remain intact on one line, which saves it, but the Metric column (~95px) wraps into 5–6 lines and the 'FY 2024' header itself breaks across two lines, so the header hierarchy looks unstable and rows become very tall.

F.why: Similar to A: generous Metric column gives 3–4 clean line wraps, all figures and units stay together on one line, and headers read straight across. Slightly narrower numeric columns than A but still comfortable, and the clipping of the last column is the unavoidable scroll trade-off.

reviewsOld.unsure: Widths are inferred from the renders; whether horizontal scrolling is acceptable in the target medium matters, since A/B/F all overflow the 359px box while C/D/E attempt to fit and fail. A and F are near-ties, with A marginally better for row evenness.
